The U.K.’s desire to become a global cryptocurrency hub appears to have collided with a barrier in the form of the country’s high-street banks. More than 10,000 complaints about banking restrictions on crypto purchases were submitted by consumers over 90 days between May and August, according to advocacy group Stand With Crypto (SWC). The country first announced its support for the industry back in 2023, when Rishi Sunak, later prime minister, was still chancellor of the exchequer for the Conservative government. That stance was reiterated by the economic secretary to the Treasury, Lucy Rigby, less than year ago under a Labour administration. “A country cannot credibly invite innovators in while allowing banks to lock consumers out,” Katie Harries, Coinbase's head of European policy, said in an email interview. “This will undoubtedly dampen the growth of the U.K.’s digital asset sector, with ramifications for associate investment here.” The 10,092 complaints submitted using an online tool by 9,800 individuals covered customers in all 650 parliamentary constituencies of the U.K., the SWC report said in a report. The findings expose a potential contradiction in the U.K.’s approach to digital assets. While the government and Financial Conduct Authority (FCA) are preparing a comprehensive regulatory regime intended to attract crypto businesses, banking restrictions can prevent consumers from accessing even regulated venues. "Bank transfers represent a crucial on-ramp to add money to their account on our platform," said Harries. “We are an FCA-registered crypto asset business, but are subject to the same blanket restrictions as the wider crypto asset sector." Lloyds Banking Group, which includes Halifax and Bank of Scotland, received the most complaints with 2,297, equivalent to 23% of the total. Barclays followed with 1,569, while NatWest Group received 1,278. The figures require some qualification. SWC collected complaints from individuals choosing to use its online tool.

items.article_context_en: Borrowing against bitcoin and earning income to build their BTC holdings are becoming priorities for long-term investors, Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca told CoinDesk. Wealthy bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 holders are increasingly treating their cryptocurrency as an asset to borrow against and generate income from, marking a shift from speculation toward private banking, according to Xapo Bank CEO Seamus Rocca. At the Gibraltar-based bank, customers are seeking cash without selling their bitcoin, putting some of their holdings into income-generating investments, or accumulating more BTC through interest paid on dollar savings, he said. “Customers are looking for yield and alpha,” Rocca told CoinDesk in an interview, pointing to demand from funds and family offices for accumulation and income products. The behavior reflects bitcoin’s growing maturity, he said. Five or six years ago, the cryptocurrency was primarily viewed as a trading and speculative asset. Today, more holders want financial services built around their existing wealth. Xapo grew out of a bitcoin custody business known for its Swiss bunker storage. Its customers include early adopters who have experienced several halvings (the periodic reductions in new bitcoin issuance), and the rallies and downturns surrounding them. The bank charges an annual membership fee of $1,000, combining dollar banking with access to bitcoin custody, investments and borrowing. Experience has pushed those customers in different directions. Some of the earliest adopters became more willing to take profits as bitcoin reached record prices, having watched gains disappear in previous downturns, Rocca said. Others, including investors who entered around 2018 and 2019, remain determined to hold and prefer borrowing against their coins when they need liquidity. For the profit-takers, selling does not necessarily mean abandoning bitcoin.

items.article_context_en: The company's head of futures and prediction markets said bitcoin, gold and oil contracts are among its fastest-growing prediction markets. Price volatility contracts tied to those assets are among the fastest-growing products in prediction markets, according to JB Mackenzie, VP and GM for futures and prediction markets at Robinhood. Sports is the largest product the platform offers, said Mackenzie at the NEXTPredict conference in New York on Thursday. However, he said there is a shift in how people use the platform. "We've now started to see price volatility contracts, such as bitcoin, crude oil, gold, start to dominate the marketplace, and they're the fastest growing products that are out there," Mackenzie said. Prediction markets allow traders to buy contracts based on whether an event will happen, with prices reflecting the market's implied probability of an outcome. A contract might ask whether bitcoin will trade above a certain price at a set time, giving traders a way to take a position without buying the cryptocurrency itself. The market has grown from its roots in elections into sports, economic data and short-term price bets. Robinhood entered the business through a partnership with Kalshi, a federally regulated prediction market exchange, and has since made event contracts a growing part of its trading platform. The expansion comes as sports contracts face legal challenges from state gambling regulators, raising questions about how much of that market will remain available. Financial contracts could offer another source of growth. Mackenzie said Robinhood's largest event contract in September wasn't tied to sports but to the Federal Reserve's interest rate decision, reflecting growing interest in economic events. Traders are also moving toward shorter contracts, particularly in crypto, where some products now settle in as little as 15 minutes. It's moved to a day, and now we're down to 15 [minutes]," he said.

items.article_context_en: Developers merged a policy change that ends the months-long embargo for flaws a chatbot could rediscover, after a summer in which AI found hundreds of bitcoin bugs before the humans did. Bitcoin Core, the software most of the bitcoin network runs on, will stop sitting on bug fixes for months when the bug is one an AI could find again, after its maintainers merged a change to the project’s security policy on Thursday. Core previously graded every reported vulnerability by severity and timed disclosure accordingly. Low-severity flaws were revealed two weeks after the next major version shipped. Medium and high ones stayed under embargo until two weeks after the last affected version reached end of life. The logic was that shipping a fix quietly and explaining it much later kept attackers from learning about a hole before the people running nodes, the computers that check and relay every bitcoin transaction, had upgraded. But the old rule was built for a world where finding a bug took skill, and the spread of AI tools has broken how that process worked. “We recently experienced an increase in the number of reports for security vulnerabilities that can be easily (re-)discovered,” Antoine Poinsot, the Chaincode Labs developer who wrote the change, said in his proposal. “This is largely due to LLMs drastically reducing the bar to find certain classes of issues or identify covert fixes.” Core can now flag a bug as easy to discover during triage, which in practice means one that “can be found with a simple prompt to an LLM.” Those bugs get a fix copied back to every version Core still supports, shipped in a point release “as soon as possible” along with a security advisory carrying some details. “For these issues that are easy to find, this is the wrong tradeoff,” the policy reads of the old embargo. “The embargo period achieves little but it delays the availability of a fixed release.” Fixes “won’t have as much ‘bake time’” in testing before they reach users, however, Poinsot wrote. Not every developer agreed on how far to go. Antoine Riard, a longtime bitcoin security researcher, wanted Core to keep the option of shipping a fix without an advisory and holding the details back case by case. “Alerting users of a security vulnerability without any details could create more risk unnecessarily,” he wrote, pointing to “a rushed migration by users who would otherwise not be affected.” A volunteer group of 16 developers calling itself the Bitcoin Red Team ran AI models across 390 bitcoin projects in about a day in late July and logged 4,962 findings, with 85 of them critical.

items.article_context_en: 23, 2026 Earlier this week, CoinDesk discussed how risk management in bitcoin is becoming increasingly popular, steadily reducing the the largest cryptocurrency’s volatility and making it more palatable to professional investors. How does its stability compare with major assets such as gold, its traditional rival, with the S&P 500, the biggest stock index, with the euro-dollar exchange rate, the most liquid fiat currency pair, and with Nvidia NVDA$211.00·Market Closed, the largest stock by market value? That comparison matters when deciding whether an asset can diversify a portfolio or increase portfolio volatility risk. It transpires there is still a long way to go before bitcoin can match the euro-dollar, gold and stock indexes in terms of stability. That’s according to a widely tracked metric called realized volatility, which measures how much an asset's price has moved over a period, such as 30 or 90 days. The gauge is the standard deviation of daily returns, usually annualized to show what a full year of such moves would look like. The higher the number, the bigger the swings and the stronger the perception that the asset is risky. Bitcoin's 90-day realized volatility stood at about 38% as of Thursday, based on CoinDesk's calculations. Its main rival, gold, is at about 23.5%. The S&P 500 sits at about 11%, so bitcoin is a little over three times as jumpy as stocks. EUR/USD, which matches the euro — the shared currency of 21 countries — against the dollar, the global reserve currency, is the steadiest of all, with a 90-day realized volatility of 4.6%. Bitcoin is roughly eight times as volatile. The currency pair’s volatility has stayed in single digits despite uncertainty over the French government debt and the resulting recent slide in the euro. Most fiat currency pairs have realized volatility below 10%.

items.article_summary_en: midterm elections are just 10 days away and bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 is approaching a period that has historically coincided with major bear-market bottoms, although this year’s recovery suggests the timing could differ. Bitcoin bottomed in January 2015, December 2018 and November 2022, shortly after the preceding midterms. Those lows arrived approximately 71, 38 and 13 days after election day, respectively. items.article_context_en: Previous bitcoin bear-market lows followed U.S. midterms, but this year’s recovery raises the possibility that the bottom arrived months earlier. midterm elections are just 10 days away and bitcoin BTC$84,459.46 is approaching a period that has historically coincided with major bear-market bottoms, although this year’s recovery suggests the timing could differ. Bitcoin bottomed in January 2015, December 2018 and November 2022, shortly after the preceding midterms. Those lows arrived approximately 71, 38 and 13 days after election day, respectively. This year, bitcoin’s lowest price so far came much earlier. Bitcoin touched $57,850 on July 1, some 125 days before the Nov. 22, the price had recovered to around $81,455, roughly 40% above that low. Historical returns also reveal substantial weakness over the broader pre-election period. Bitcoin fell approximately 29% in the six months before the 2018 midterms and 37% before the 2022 vote. Technology stocks have also experienced weakness around midterms. The Invesco QQQ Trust fell roughly 23% from the end of September to its December 2018 low, with much of the decline occurring after election day. It also dropped 17% in the three months preceding the 2022 vote. However, QQQ gained 17% over the six months before the 2014 midterms, showing the pattern is not entirely consistent.
